ComoUsar.title: How to Use the Text Counter
ComoUsar.intro: Using Use Count Me is simple and instant. No registration or extension installation is required:

steps.step1Text: Enter the content directly into the main text box.
steps.step2Title: Check the metrics in real time:
steps.step2Text: Character counts (with and without spaces), words, and sentences are updated automatically as you type.

actions.copyText: Sends the content directly to your device's clipboard.
actions.clearText: Empties the text area so you can start a new count.
actions.formatText: Quickly switch the text to uppercase (UPPERCASE) or lowercase (lowercase).

ComoUsar.conclusion: Because the tool focuses on accurate metrics and efficiency, we have kept the interface clean and straightforward, making it ideal for quickly reviewing academic papers, social media posts, and articles.

Etimologia.title: Etymology: The Origins of the Words We Count
Etimologia.intro: Have you ever wondered where the terms we use every day when writing a document come from? The history behind the vocabulary of writing is fascinating and dates back to classical antiquity.
Etimologia.palavraText: comes from the Vulgar Latin paraula, which in turn derives from the Classical Latin parabola (meaning "comparison," "discourse," or "allegory"). The latter word has roots in the Ancient Greek parabolē (parabolē), meaning "to place beside" or "to compare." Over the centuries, the term evolved from the concept of comparison to designate the basic unit of speech and writing.
Etimologia.textoText: comes from the Latin textus, which literally means "fabric," "weave," or "woven material." The term derives from the Latin verb texere ("to weave"). The analogy is both poetic and precise: just as individual threads are woven together to form cloth, words and sentences are woven together by the author to create a coherent work.
Etimologia.caractereText: (or character) comes from the Ancient Greek kharaktēr, a term used for the tool used to engrave, mark, or stamp coins and symbols. Later, it came to mean the engraved sign itself or the distinctive mark of something—giving rise both to the typographical characters we count and to the concept of human "character."

FAQ.title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
FAQ.q1Title: Is the text I type saved on any server?
FAQ.q1Text: All processing is performed exclusively in your own browser (client-side). The text you type is not sent to, read by, or stored on any external server. We only use local sessionStorage to prevent you from losing your progress if you accidentally reload the page, but everything is deleted when you close the tab.
FAQ.q2Text: The tool is 100% free with no usage limits. You do not need to create an account, log in, or provide personal information to use all its features.
FAQ.q3Title: How are words and sentences counted?
FAQ.q3Text: The word count identifies the spaces and punctuation marks that separate terms. The sentence count identifies the periods, question marks, and exclamation marks that delimit each sentence in your text.
FAQ.q4Title: Can I use the tool on my phone?
FAQ.q4Text: The website layout is fully responsive and adapted to work well on computers, tablets, and smartphones.

PqUsar.title: Why Use a Word and Character Counter?
PqUsar.intro: In many everyday situations, we need to produce content that meets strict length limits. Counting words or characters manually is inefficient and prone to errors. Use Count Me automates this process with absolute accuracy.

applications.socialText: Each platform has its own text limits, such as X/Twitter, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Meta Ads. Using the counter prevents your captions or ads from being cut off.
applications.academicText: Essays, abstracts, and articles often require a minimum or maximum number of words to comply with academic standards.
applications.seoText: Writers and marketing professionals need to keep meta descriptions, article titles, and blog posts within the ideal length for search engines.
applications.formsText: Applications for jobs, scholarships, or project submissions often impose strict limits on text fields.

PqUsar.privacy: In addition to providing instant metrics, the tool runs entirely locally in your browser, ensuring privacy for confidential drafts or personal documents.

VisaoAutor.title: The Author's Perspective and Motivation
VisaoAutor.intro: Use Count Me was created from the desire to combine practical utility with continuous improvement in modern web development.

items.logicText: Implementation of real-time string manipulation and predictable state management with React.
items.archText: Exploration of the App Router, modular component organization, and optimization for SEO and performance.
items.uxText: Building a clean and responsive design with CSS, focused on a straightforward user experience.
items.seoText: Practical application of search engine optimization strategies using the Next.js Metadata API, structured data architecture, and navigation files such as sitemap.xml and robots.txt for maximum organic visibility.
items.lifecycleText: From the conception of the code to deployment in production, with preparation for integrating analytics and advertisements.

VisaoAutor.conclusion: Besides serving as a functional everyday tool, this project is an important milestone in building my portfolio as a developer.

Sobre.title: About Use Count Me
Sobre.intro: Use Count Me is a fast, free, and intuitive web tool created to simplify text counting and manipulation in your daily routine.
Sobre.proposalText1: Whether writing an essay, tweaking a social media post, or checking character limits on a document, Use Count Me was designed to deliver accurate real-time metrics without hassle.
Sobre.proposalText2: Built with Next.js, TypeScript, and React, all text processing happens directly in your browser. This ensures instant speed and total data privacy.

features.metricsText: Character count (with and without spaces), word count, and sentence count.
features.formattingText: Quick conversion to uppercase and lowercase.
features.actionsText: One-click buttons to copy text and clear the workspace.

BoringSites.title: Boring Sites
BoringSites.subtitle: Building a boring site
BoringSites.introText: If you're a developer, you've probably come across the term 'boring site'—especially if you follow tech content in English. There are tons of videos claiming you can make $1,000/month building these simple tools. So, well... here's my honest take on this category of websites, how to build them, and how monetizing them actually works.
BoringSites.whatAreText: Boring sites are super simple, single-purpose web utilities. They're completely free online tools made for one quick task: counting words, changing text case, rolling a die, generating text, you name it. They're the kind of site people randomly need out of nowhere. For instance, an English student writing an essay with a 150-word minimum will pop their text into an online word counter instead of manually counting every single word. Honestly, I've been that student many times—and I still am, since I'm currently taking English classes!
BoringSites.monetizationText: You're probably wondering if you can actually make money with these sites, and the short answer is yes! Before getting into details, keep in mind I'll share my hands-on experience with Use Count Me later on. Every website has running costs—hosting, domain registration, and so on. So how does a free, simple utility make a profit? Ads. The business model relies on search intent: users Google a tool, click your top link, ads render, they use the tool, and leave. By the end of the month, high ad impressions hopefully turn into some decent pocket money.
BoringSites.adsOriginTitle: Where Do the Ads Come From?
BoringSites.adsOriginText: The ads shown on the site come from Google AdSense. You submit your site and wait anywhere from a few days to four weeks for an approval or rejection email. However, AdSense has strict guidelines: you must have Privacy Policy and About pages, plus actual substantial content. That's the main bottleneck for utility tools like Use Count Me—what kind of 'articles' are you supposed to put on a word counter? Write about the history of counting words? Because of this lack of written content, Use Count Me got rejected by AdSense after a week of waiting. And that's literally why I'm writing this article right now: to add valuable content and get approved on my next attempt!
BoringSites.realityText: Boring sites aren't a get-rich-quick scheme for devs. Realistically, it takes several months before you see any meaningful revenue. Running paid ads makes zero sense here, as you'd be spending money on traffic just to earn fractions of a cent on ad impressions. It's all about organic traffic through solid SEO.
BoringSites.whyBuiltTitle: Why Did I Build Use Count Me?
BoringSites.whyBuiltText: Use Count Me is my second live production project. My first project was a single-page expense management app packed with cool tech, but it took way too long to finish. I wanted to level up my Next.js, React, and production skills without spending months on a single build, so I went with a boring site. Honestly? Even though it gave me quite a headache (a story I share in detail on this <pageLink>page</pageLink>), I learned a ton. I'm learning how to maintain a real app online, practicing hands-on SEO, launching my first multi-language project in English, Portuguese, and Spanish, and making plenty of mistakes I can grow from.

ContadorPalavras.title: Word Counter
ContadorPalavras.subtitle: My experience building a word counter website
ContadorPalavras.beginningText: The backstory behind why I built Use Count Me is already covered on this <boringSitesLink>page</boringSitesLink>, so I'll get straight to the point: code development was actually the easiest part. Once I launched it online, it was nonstop headaches. Right when I thought everything was finished and I could finally chill, a brand-new issue would pop up. It's tough!
ContadorPalavras.searchConsoleText: To show up on Google, you have to submit your site to Google Search Console so its pages can get indexed. For that to happen smoothly, you need proper sitemap.xml and robots.txt files. The robots file tells Googlebot what it can crawl, while the sitemap lists all valid routes. When I submitted my site, Search Console couldn't find the sitemap, so I had to rebuild it. On top of that, I had to resize my favicon to 512x512 so Google search results would display the icon properly.
ContadorPalavras.hostingText: My next big mess was hosting. Originally, I deployed Use Count Me on Vercel using their free Hobby plan. I assumed it was free based on low traffic volume, but in reality, that tier is strictly for non-commercial projects. I actually went and read the Terms of Service (who would've thought?), only to discover Vercel could take down my site anytime without notice. To avoid having my site pulled once ads were running, I migrated everything to a Hostinger VPS I already had. That meant setting up Docker, Nginx, and converting the app to static exports so it runs super light. I also had to tweak the middleware: prior to v1.1.8, the site detected the user's browser language and redirected to /pt, /en, or /es. Now, it skips detection and defaults everyone straight to /en.
ContadorPalavras.adsenseText: When I submitted the site to Google AdSense, I definitely didn't expect to wait a full week for a review—I figured it'd take two or three days tops. The answer? Rejected! It got turned down for lack of content. So I am literally writing this article and this other <boringSitesLink>page</boringSitesLink> right now just to re-apply and pass the AdSense check.
ContadorPalavras.worthItText: Without a doubt, 100% worth it! I made plenty of mistakes during development—after all, this is only my second production project. I messed up component organization in React (where UI elements are supposed to be modular, Lego-like components). I didn't make reusable components for my header, footer, or navbar... so yeah, I am literally copy-pasting the same code blocks into every single new page I build! Why haven't I fixed it? Pure laziness! I'd have to refactor the HTML and CSS across all existing pages. Another mistake was hosting on Vercel thinking commercial use was free—there's no such thing as a free lunch. But every mistake I made, whether in code or deployment, is a huge lesson for my upcoming projects. Building Use Count Me was super fun, and if you made it this far into my rambling, I'm genuinely impressed! With that said... on to the next project!
